#Building the ensemble function
lr.ensemble <- function(models, oob.sets, new.data, cutoff = best_cutoff_lr) { #setting parameters
  
  #Computing F1 for each model using its out-of-bag data
  f1s <- sapply(1:length(models), function(i) {
    model <- models[[i]]
    oob.data <- oob.sets[[i]]
    probs <- predict(model, newdata = oob.data, type = "response")
    preds <- ifelse(probs > cutoff, "TRUE", "FALSE")
    f1_score(oob.data$Revenue, preds)
  })
  
  weights <- f1s / sum(f1s) #Normalizing weights to add to 1
  
  predictions <- sapply(models, function(model) { #Predict with each model on new data
    predict(model, newdata = new.data, type = "response")
  })
  
  if (is.vector(predictions)) { #Making sure predictions are in matrix form
    predictions <- matrix(predictions, nrow = 1)
  }
  
  weighted.probs <- predictions %*% weights #Applying weights
  as.vector(weighted.probs)
}

Evaluation

Now, I will evaluate my ensemble.

lr_ensemble_probs <- lr.ensemble(lr_models, out.of.bag, test_logreg, cutoff = best_cutoff_lr)
lr_ensemble_preds <- ifelse(lr_ensemble_probs > best_cutoff_lr, "TRUE", "FALSE")

#AUC
roc_lr <- roc(response = test_logreg$Revenue, predictor = lr_ensemble_probs,
               levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
auc_lr_test <- auc(roc_lr)

#F1
f1_lr_test <- f1_score(test_logreg$Revenue, lr_ensemble_preds)

auc_lr_test
## Area under the curve: 0.9173
f1_lr_test
## [1] 0.5817556

This model achieved an AUC of 0.9173 and an F1 score of 0.5818. The AUC is strong and comparable to kNN’s bagged model (AUC = 0.9139), indicating that logistic regression, despite its far simpler linear structure, ranks converting sessions above non-converting ones nearly as well as the more instance-based kNN approach.

The F1 score (0.5818), however, is somewhat lower than kNN’s bagged F1 (0.6237), suggesting that at the classification threshold ultimately selected, logistic regression’s precision/recall balance on the minority purchasing class is less favorable than kNN’s. This gap between AUC and weaker F1 is a useful reminder of why both metrics were tracked throughout this project, a model can rank outcomes well overall while still underperforming at the threshold used to make classification decisions. Since both kNN and logistic regression were trained on undersampled data, this comparison does not directly test how differently the two algorithms handle class imbalance on their own; that distinction will be more meaningfully evaluated once the decision tree, which instead used case weights on the full dataset, is complete.

Decision Tree

The third model I will build is a decision tree, using the C5.0 algorithm. This rule-based, non-parametric algorithm recursively splits the data into subgroups based on the features that most effectively separate the target classes, producing interpretable if-then rules. Unlike kNN and logistic regression, the tree requires no transformation, standardization, or encoding, since C5.0 splits directly on categorical variables and makes no distributional assumptions, which is why df_tree retains the original variables.

As discussed in Data Cleaning, I will address class imbalance here using case weights rather than undersampling, up-weighting the minority (TRUE) class during training without discarding rows. I considered a cost matrix, since C5.0 supports this natively, but it does not produce valid class probabilities when applied, which would break AUC computation and disrupt consistency across models.

Because C5.0’s trials parameter builds a sequence of trees, each trained to correct the errors of the prior trees, and combines their predictions via a weighted vote, boosting itself constitutes a homogeneous ensemble of decision trees, satisfying the same underlying requirement as bagging while using a combination mechanism native to this specific algorithm. I will therefore prioritize tuning and applying boosting over building a separate manual bagging loop, since it is both more idiomatic to C5.0 and more efficient to implement. I will fit a single case-weighted baseline model, then tune trials to build the final decision tree ensemble for this section.

Case Weight Setup

To address class imbalance, I will assign each observation a case weight based on the inverse frequency of its class, giving the minority “TRUE” (purchase) class a proportionally higher weight than the majority “FALSE” class. These weights will be passed directly into the C5.0 model during training, so that misclassifying a purchasing session is treated as more costly than misclassifying a non-purchasing session.

class_counts <- table(train_tree$Revenue)
weight_true <- sum(class_counts) / (2 * class_counts["TRUE"])
weight_false <- sum(class_counts) / (2 * class_counts["FALSE"])

case_weights <- ifelse(train_tree$Revenue == "TRUE", weight_true, weight_false)

Baseline Model

Before applying boosting, I will first fit a single case-weighted decision tree with no boosting iterations evaluated once on the test set at a standard 0.5 threshold. This baseline model serves as the reference point against which the boosted ensemble will later be compared, allowing me to assess whether boosting meaningfully improves on a single decision tree for this dataset.

tree_baseline <- C5.0(Revenue ~ ., data = train_tree, weights = case_weights)

#Predicting probabilities on the test set
tree_baseline_probs <- predict(tree_baseline, newdata = test_tree, type = "prob")[, "TRUE"]

#Converting probabilities to class predictions at a 0.5 threshold
tree_baseline_preds <- ifelse(tree_baseline_probs > 0.5, "TRUE", "FALSE")

#AUC
roc_tree_baseline <- roc(response = test_tree$Revenue, predictor = tree_baseline_probs,
                          levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
auc_tree_baseline <- auc(roc_tree_baseline)

#F1
f1_tree_baseline <- f1_score(test_tree$Revenue, tree_baseline_preds)

auc_tree_baseline
## Area under the curve: 0.9193
f1_tree_baseline
## [1] 0.6336822

The single case-weighted decision tree achieved an AUC of 0.9193 and an F1 of 0.6337, evaluated on the test set at a standard 0.5 threshold. This is a notably strong baseline, already outperforming both the bagged kNN ensemble (AUC = 0.9139, F1 = 0.6237) and the bagged logistic regression ensemble (AUC = 0.9173, F1 = 0.5818) on both metrics, despite being a single, unensembled model trained on the full, imbalanced dataset rather than an undersampled or bootstrap-aggregated one.

This result is particularly interesting because, as noted, decison trees can often be adjusted for imbalance fairly directly, in contrast to kNN’s greater sensitivity to imbalance by construction. The decision tree’s strong single-model performance here, achieved purely through case weighting rather than undersampling, offers early support for that expectation. Even before any ensembling is applied, case weighting on the full training set appears to be at least as effective as undersampling was for the other two algorithms, and possibly more so given the tree’s higher baseline F1. Whether boosting improves on this already-strong result further remains to be seen in the following subsection.

Tuning Trials

I will tune the number of boosting iterations (trials) using 10-fold cross-validation on train_tree, consistent with my approach for kNN. I begin testing at trials = 5, 10, 15, 20, since this range is wide enough to reveal whether performance is still improving or has started to decline, while keeping the initial search computationally reasonable.

#Tuning trials via 10-fold CV 
set.seed(999)
n_folds <- 10
trials_candidates <- c(5, 10, 15, 20)

folds_tree <- sample(rep(1:n_folds, length.out = nrow(train_tree)))

cv_results_tree <- data.frame(trials = trials_candidates, mean_f1 = NA)

for (t in trials_candidates) {
  fold_f1s <- numeric(n_folds)
  
  for (fold in 1:n_folds) {
    cv_train_tree <- train_tree[folds_tree != fold, ]
    cv_val_tree   <- train_tree[folds_tree == fold, ]
    cv_train_weights <- case_weights[folds_tree != fold]
    
    model <- C5.0(Revenue ~ ., data = cv_train_tree, weights = cv_train_weights, trials = t)
    
    probs <- predict(model, newdata = cv_val_tree, type = "prob")[, "TRUE"]
    preds <- ifelse(probs > 0.5, "TRUE", "FALSE")
    
    fold_f1s[fold] <- f1_score(cv_val_tree$Revenue, preds)
  }
  
  cv_results_tree$mean_f1[cv_results_tree$trials == t] <- mean(fold_f1s)
}

cv_results_tree
##   trials   mean_f1
## 1      5 0.6336030
## 2     10 0.6465220
## 3     15 0.6428797
## 4     20 0.6513450
best_trials <- cv_results_tree$trials[which.max(cv_results_tree$mean_f1)]
best_trials
## [1] 20

To ensure the true optimum was not missed at the upper boundary of the initial search, and since F1 continued to improve through trials = 20, I will extend the range of candidate trials values further (c(20, 30, 40, 50)) and re-run the same 10-fold cross-validation procedure.

#Tuning trials via 10-fold CV 
set.seed(996)
n_folds <- 10
trials_candidates <- c(20, 30, 40, 50)

folds_tree <- sample(rep(1:n_folds, length.out = nrow(train_tree)))

cv_results_tree <- data.frame(trials = trials_candidates, mean_f1 = NA)

for (t in trials_candidates) {
  fold_f1s <- numeric(n_folds)
  
  for (fold in 1:n_folds) {
    cv_train_tree <- train_tree[folds_tree != fold, ]
    cv_val_tree   <- train_tree[folds_tree == fold, ]
    cv_train_weights <- case_weights[folds_tree != fold]
    
    model <- C5.0(Revenue ~ ., data = cv_train_tree, weights = cv_train_weights, trials = t)
    
    probs <- predict(model, newdata = cv_val_tree, type = "prob")[, "TRUE"]
    preds <- ifelse(probs > 0.5, "TRUE", "FALSE")
    
    fold_f1s[fold] <- f1_score(cv_val_tree$Revenue, preds)
  }
  
  cv_results_tree$mean_f1[cv_results_tree$trials == t] <- mean(fold_f1s)
}

cv_results_tree
##   trials   mean_f1
## 1     20 0.6359216
## 2     30 0.6444820
## 3     40 0.6432400
## 4     50 0.6417234
best_trials <- cv_results_tree$trials[which.max(cv_results_tree$mean_f1)]
best_trials
## [1] 30

I will lock in the optimal trial amount as 30.

best_trials <- 30

Boosting

Now, I will boost the full model with the best_trials (30), evaluate on the test set, and compare to the unboosted model.

tree_boosted_final <- C5.0(Revenue ~ ., data = train_tree, weights = case_weights, trials = best_trials)

boosted_probs_final <- predict(tree_boosted_final, newdata = test_tree, type = "prob")[, "TRUE"]
boosted_preds_final <- ifelse(boosted_probs_final > 0.5, "TRUE", "FALSE")

roc_boosted_final <- roc(response = test_tree$Revenue, predictor = boosted_probs_final,
                          levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
auc_tree_boosted <- auc(roc_boosted_final)
f1_tree_boosted <- f1_score(test_tree$Revenue, boosted_preds_final)

auc_tree_boosted
## Area under the curve: 0.9298
f1_tree_boosted
## [1] 0.6684783

Evaluation

Boosting produced a meaningful improvement over the single-tree baseline: AUC increased from 0.9193 to 0.9298, and F1 increased from 0.6337 to 0.6685, a gain of over three F1 points. This is a more substantial improvement than bagging provided for kNN, which makes intuitive sense given the two techniques’ different mechanisms; bagging primarily reduces variance by averaging over resampled models, which offers less benefit when the initial model is already relatively stable, whereas boosting iteratively corrects the specific errors of prior trees, allowing it to capture patterns a single tree missed entirely rather than simply smoothing over prediction noise.

With this result, the boosted decision tree (AUC = 0.9298, F1 = 0.6685) outperforms both the bagged kNN ensemble (AUC = 0.9139, F1 = 0.6237) and the bagged logistic regression ensemble (AUC = 0.9173, F1 = 0.5818) on both metrics, making it the strongest individual model built in this project. This finalized boosted tree will be carried forward into the final cross-model Evaluation and the heterogeneous Ensemble section.

Ensemble

In this final modeling section, I will build a heterogeneous ensemble combining the three finalized models built throughout this report: the bagged kNN (PCA reduced) model, the bagged logistic regression ensemble, and the boosted decision tree. Unlike the homogeneous ensembles built for each individual algorithm, this ensemble combines structurally different models, each with its own assumptions and approach to handling class imbalance, to see whether blending them produces a more accurate or more stable prediction than any single algorithm alone.

Each model’s predicted probabilities will be combined via a weighted average, with weights determined by each model’s F1 on its own test set. Weighting by F1 instead of AUC produces more differentiated results than the AUC-based weighting would have, reflecting the wider spread in F1 performance across the three models compared to their relatively similar AUC scores. Also, the F1 more directly reflects each model’s real-world classification performance at an actual decision threshold, the outcome this project is ultimately concerned with. Because all three test sets were derived from the same underlying rows using identical train/test indices, Revenue is identical across all three and can be used interchangeably to score the combined ensemble. I will then tune the ensemble’s classification cutoff by sweeping a range of candidate values and selecting whichever maximizes F1, before reporting the finalized ensemble’s AUC and F1 as the concluding result of this project’s modeling work.

I will begin by building the base model with the weights.

#Base model
het.ensemble <- function(knn_probs, lr_probs, tree_probs, weight_knn, weight_lr, weight_tree) {
  weight_knn * knn_probs + weight_lr * lr_probs + weight_tree * tree_probs
}

#Determining weights
weight_knn <- f1_bag_test / (f1_bag_test + f1_lr_test + f1_tree_boosted)
weight_lr <- f1_lr_test / (f1_bag_test + f1_lr_test + f1_tree_boosted)
weight_tree <- f1_tree_boosted / (f1_bag_test + f1_lr_test + f1_tree_boosted)

cat("kNN weight:", round(weight_knn, 3), "\n")
## kNN weight: 0.333
cat("LR weight:", round(weight_lr, 3), "\n")
## LR weight: 0.31
cat("Tree weight:", round(weight_tree, 3), "\n")
## Tree weight: 0.357

The decision tree receives the largest weight (0.357), consistent with its clear F1 advantage, while logistic regression receives the smallest weight (0.31), reflecting its comparatively weaker precision-recall balance on the minority purchasing class. kNN falls in between (0.333).

Tuning

Now, I will tune the ensemble’s classification cutoff by sweeping a range of candidate values and selecting whichever maximizes F1 on the combined predicted probabilities. This range is centered around the conventional 0.5 threshold- it goes a little higher and a little lower.

het_test_probs <- het.ensemble(bag_prob_avg, lr_ensemble_probs, boosted_probs_final,
                                 weight_knn, weight_lr, weight_tree)

het_cutoff_candidates <- seq(0.20, 0.60, by = 0.05)
het_f1_by_cutoff <- numeric(length(het_cutoff_candidates))

for (c in seq_along(het_cutoff_candidates)) {
  cutoff_val <- het_cutoff_candidates[c]
  preds <- ifelse(het_test_probs > cutoff_val, "TRUE", "FALSE")
  het_f1_by_cutoff[c] <- f1_score(test_knn_pca$Revenue, preds)
}

data.frame(cutoff = het_cutoff_candidates, het_f1 = het_f1_by_cutoff)

het_cutoff_candidates <- seq(0.50, 0.80, by = 0.05)

Evaluation

het_final_preds <- ifelse(het_test_probs > best_het_cutoff, "TRUE", "FALSE")

#AUC
roc_het <- roc(response = test_tree$Revenue, predictor = het_test_probs,
                levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)

The heterogeneous ensemble achieved a final AUC of 0.9318 and F1 of 0.6683 on the test set, evaluated at a tuned cutoff of 0.6. This represents the highest AUC of any model built in this project, exceeding even the boosted decision tree’s AUC of 0.9298, while its F1 is nearly identical to the tree’s (0.6685), a difference of only 2^{-4}. This result closely matches my Introduction expectation that the ensemble would outperform any single model, but not dramatically, producing a more stable improvement rather than a dramatic jump in predictive power.

Strengths and Weaknesses of Each Model

kNN performed respectably (AUC =0.9139, F1 = 0.6237) once features were log-transformed, standardized, and reduced via PCA, but this performance came at the cost of the heaviest preprocessing burden of the three algorithms, requiring careful handling to be competitive at all. As expected from the Introduction, kNN offers no interpretability, its predictions come from proximity to past sessions rather than any explainable rule, making it the least useful of the three models for generating actionable business insight, despite performing on par with the other algorithms on both metrics.

Logistic regression offers the clearest theoretical interpretability of the three, its fitted coefficients can, in principle, be converted directly into odds ratios that a stakeholder could act on. This report did not extract or interpret those specific coefficients, focusing instead on predictive performance, but this remains a structural advantage of the algorithm that could be pursued in future work. Despite this potential for interpretability, logistic regression produced the weakest F1 score of the three individual models (0.5818) despite a strong AUC (0.9173), suggesting its linear structure ranks sessions by purchase likelihood well overall, but is comparatively less precise at the specific threshold used for classification.

The decision tree, boosted through 30 sequential iterations, was the strongest individual model on both metrics (AUC = 0.9298, F1 = 0.6685). Like logistic regression, its rule-based, if-then structure offers a theoretical interpretability advantage over kNN, though this report did not extract the specific split rules generated. Its use of case weights rather than undersampling allowed it to train on the full dataset without discarding any rows, and boosting provided a substantially larger performance gain over its single-tree baseline than bagging did for either kNN or logistic regression, since boosting directly and iteratively corrects prior errors rather than simply averaging over independently resampled fits.

Best Model and Conclusion

The heterogeneous ensemble achieved the highest AUC of any model built in this project (0.9318), narrowly exceeding even the boosted decision tree’s AUC (0.9298), while its F1 score (0.6683) is nearly identical to the tree’s alone (0.6685), a difference of only 2^{-4}. This result closely matches my Introduction expectation that combining models with different strengths would yield a modest improvement rather than a dramatic jump in performance. Notably, the boosted decision tree alone remains highly competitive with the full ensemble, suggesting that for this dataset, a single well-tuned, boosted tree captures nearly all of the achievable predictive signal on its own.

Given its combination of the strongest overall performance and meaningful (if unexamined in this report) rule-based interpretability, the boosted decision tree stands out as the most practically useful model on its own, while the heterogeneous ensemble offers a small additional edge in ranking ability (AUC) at the cost of losing the tree’s relative simplicity. For a business stakeholder prioritizing both accuracy and explainability, the boosted decision tree is likely the more actionable choice; for a use case where even a small gain in predictive accuracy meaningfully matters, such as at very large scale, the ensemble’s marginal AUC advantage may justify its added complexity.

Returning to the original research question, browsing behavior captured during a single e-commerce session, particularly PageValues, exit and bounce rates, and product-page engagement, does meaningfully predict purchase intent, and a boosted decision tree or heterogeneous ensemble of classic algorithms identifies this intent well. Consistent with expectations set out at the start of this project, class imbalance shaped every stage of this analysis, from the choice of evaluation metrics to the imbalance-handling strategy used for each algorithm, and PageValues emerged, as anticipated, as a dominant predictor. The comparatively modest gains from ensembling further suggest that for this dataset, the underlying signal already present in the browsing behavior data, rather than the specific choice of algorithm, is the primary driver of predictive performance.
